# Book I, Proposition 38

*Triangles on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal*

> Triangles which are on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal to one another.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/38-idea.svg" alt="Two triangles on equal bases (red) and between the same parallels (blue) are equal in area (yellow), however differently they lean." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Two triangles on equal bases (red) and between the same parallels (blue) are equal in area (yellow), however differently they lean.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/38.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.38, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ABC, DEF be triangles on equal bases BC, EF and in the same parallels BF, AD;

I say that the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF.

For let AD be produced in both directions to G, H; through B let BG be drawn parallel to CA, [I. 31] and through F let FH be drawn parallel to DE.

Then each of the figures GBCA, DEFH is a parallelogram; and GBCA is equal to DEFH; for they are on equal bases BC, EF and in the same parallels BF, GH. [I. 36]

Moreover the triangle ABC is half of the parallelogram GBCA; for the diameter AB bisects it. [I. 34]

And the triangle FED is half of the parallelogram DEFH; for the diameter DF bisects it. [I. 34]

[But the halves of equal things are equal to one another.]

Therefore the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop38.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop38.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- Triangles which are on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop38 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hbase : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖)
    (hpar : ∃ L M : Line, Parallel L M ∧ OnLine A L ∧ OnLine D L ∧
      OnLine B M ∧ OnLine C M ∧ OnLine E M ∧ OnLine F M) :
    △ A B C = △ D E F := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be triangles on equal bases BC, EF and in the same parallels BF, AD;
  obtain ⟨AD, BF, hAD_BF, hA, hD, hB, hC, hE, hF⟩ := hpar
  -- I say that the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF.
  -- For let AD be produced in both directions to G, H; through B let BG be drawn parallel to
  -- CA, [I. 31] and through F let FH be drawn parallel to DE.
  /- G and H are where the parallels BG and FH meet AD (`Prop31.parallelogram`,
     which cites I.30 for the meeting). -/
  obtain ⟨G, hG, hACBG⟩ := Prop31.parallelogram hAD_BF hA hC hB hABC.ne₂₃.symm
  obtain ⟨H, hH, hDEFH⟩ := Prop31.parallelogram hAD_BF hD hE hF hDEF.ne₂₃
  -- Then each of the figures GBCA, DEFH is a parallelogram; and GBCA is equal to DEFH; for
  -- they are on equal bases BC, EF and in the same parallels BF, GH. [I. 36]
  have hGBCA : Parallelogram G B C A := hACBG.reverse.rotate
  have h36 : quadArea G B C A = quadArea D E F H :=
    Prop36 hGBCA hDEFH hbase ⟨AD, hG, hA, hD, hH⟩ ⟨BF, hB, hC, hE, hF⟩
  -- Moreover the triangle ABC is half of the parallelogram GBCA; for the diameter AB bisects
  -- it. [I. 34]
  have h₁ : quadArea G B C A = △ A B C + △ A B C := by
    rw [← hGBCA.quadArea_rotate, area_bca A B C]
    exact Prop34.bisect hGBCA.rotate
  -- And the triangle FED is half of the parallelogram DEFH; for the diameter DF bisects
  -- it. [I. 34]
  have h₂ : quadArea D E F H = △ F E D + △ F E D := by
    rw [area_cba F E D]
    exact Prop34.bisect hDEFH
  -- [But the halves of equal things are equal to one another.]
  have heq : △ A B C = △ F E D := Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq (h₁.symm.trans (h36.trans h₂))
  -- Therefore the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF.
  rw [heq, area_cba F E D]
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**Two bases in place of one.** Euclid repeats I.37 with the triangles set apart on equal bases BC, EF. He completes the parallelograms GBCA and DEFH, which I.36 now makes equal, and the diameters AB and DF halve them (I.34). J. L. Heiberg brackets the sentence on halves here too, as Heath notes under I.37, and the little argument we gave there takes the step again. Our statement lets the bases overlap or share an end, and, as I.42 will want, the two vertices be one point; I.36 covers every arrangement.

**"Assumed in order to prove VI. 1."** Proclus thought Euclid had proved all four of I.35–I.38 at once in VI.1, where triangles and parallelograms of the same altitude are to one another as their bases, "for of course to be of the same altitude is equivalent to being in the same parallels"; most readers, he says, had missed it (Heath, vol. 1, p. 334). Heath answers: "It is true that VI. 1 generalises these propositions, but it must be observed that it does not prove the propositions themselves, as Proclus seems to imply; they are in fact assumed in order to prove VI. 1" (p. 334). The equalities come first, and Book VI's ratios are built on them.

**The triangles of I.24, by area.** Heron, in an-Nairīzī, places here a theorem Proclus gives under I.24. When two triangles have two sides equal to two sides, "*if the sum of the two angles contained by the equal sides is equal to two right angles, the two triangles are equal to one another*" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 334); if the sum is less, the one with the greater angle is the greater, and if more, the one with the less. For the first case Heron copies one triangle onto a side of the other, its vertex on the parallel to that side through the other's, and I.37 makes them equal. I.24 compared the bases of such triangles; Heron compares their areas.

**The modern way.** Put BF on the x-axis and AD on the straight line y = h, with h positive: the triangles have areas ½·BC·h and ½·EF·h, equal because BC = EF. With the height fixed the area goes with the base, as VI.1 says.

## Further reading

- For where cutting and pasting runs out, Martin Aigner and Günter M. Ziegler's [*Proofs from THE BOOK*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-662-57265-8) (2018), the chapter "Hilbert's third problem: decomposing polyhedra", which shows why it always works for polygons of equal area, as here, but fails for solids.
- For the order Heath insists on, these equalities first and the ratios of VI.1 built on them, Ian Mueller's [*Philosophy of Mathematics and Deductive Structure in Euclid's Elements*](https://openlibrary.org/books/OL7640284M) (1981), which charts which propositions each one rests on, book by book.
